entries.clue: Rabbit on book lover's top smeared with honey (6)

indicatorNotes.top: The top of a word is where it starts, so its opening letter is all that is taken.
indicatorNotes.smeared with: Anything smeared with honey wears it right round the outside, so the sweet word closes over the letters before it.

blocks.note: honey is what one lover calls another, and babe is the same endearment; the word opens after its third letter
B is the standard short form for book
the opening letter of the word, which is all the instruction beside it wants

annotation.surface: A rabbit sitting on a bookworm's shirt, the whole thing sticky with honey.
annotation.walkthrough: Honey is the endearment here rather than the jar, which is why it can wrap round anything. To rabbit on is British for talking without a pause, from the rhyming slang rabbit and pork, talk.
annotation.definitionFit: To rabbit on is to talk at length without saying much, which is exactly the sense of babble used of a person.

entries.clue: Spike troubles island country (8)

blocks.note: the spike on a hook or a length of wire is its barb
an ado is a fuss or a bother, and more than one gives ados

annotation.surface: A man called Spike making trouble for a small nation.
annotation.walkthrough: Ado for a fuss survives mainly in Much Ado About Nothing and in crosswords, and its plural is the piece that finishes the name. Barbados is the easternmost Caribbean island, independent of Britain since 1966 and a republic since 2021.
annotation.definitionFit: Barbados is a sovereign state occupying one Caribbean island, so island country names its kind exactly.

entries.clue: Naughty bits cleaned here – wait at end of street (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition says what the answer is for instead of naming it, so a whole phrase stands where a noun would.

indicatorNotes.at end of: What sits at the end of a word is its final letter, and that letter alone is taken.

blocks.note: to bide is to wait, the verb kept alive by bide your time
the last letter of the word

annotation.surface: A place down the road where the rude bits get washed.
annotation.walkthrough: Bide is the old verb for wait, and the dash is the only join between the two halves of the clue. A bidet is the low basin French bathrooms keep beside the lavatory.
annotation.definitionFit: A bidet is the low basin you sit astride to wash the genitals and behind, so the phrase names the job it exists for.

entries.clue: Double lavatory fitted on car – enjoy! (9)

indicatorNotes.fitted on: In a down entry a thing fitted on another rests above it, so the lavatory's letters go on top of the car's.

blocks.note: the everyday British word for the lavatory
the Ka was Ford's smallest hatchback, sold in Britain from 1996
to like a thing is to enjoy it

annotation.surface: A car fitted with a twin lavatory, offered up as a treat.
annotation.walkthrough: Double is the noun — a person so like another they could stand in for them — where the surface wants the adjective for a pair of lavatories. The Ford Ka is the car crosswords reach for when two letters are wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: A lookalike could be mistaken for somebody else, which is what is meant by calling one person another's double.

entries.clue: Illicit drug bundle – shipping hazard (3,4)

blocks.note: ice is the street name for crystal methamphetamine
a pack is a bundle made up for carrying

annotation.surface: A consignment of smuggled drugs putting a ship at risk.
annotation.walkthrough: Ice as a drug is what lets the frozen answer hide behind a smuggling story. The floes meant here are the ones driven together at sea, not the cold compress for a swollen ankle.
annotation.definitionFit: An ice pack is a mass of floating floes packed together, which is what has always threatened ships in polar water.

entries.clue: Hint of frigidity about Pike? (5)

blocks.note: c for circa, the about a historian puts in front of a date
in northern England a pike is a hill with a peak, as in Scafell Pike

annotation.surface: A cold feeling about a man named Pike.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital dresses Pike as a surname when it is the northern word for a peaked hill, and the question mark admits it is one hill among many. Scafell Pike, the highest in England, is the famous one.
annotation.definitionFit: A chill is cold felt rather than measured, the touch of it in the air, which is frigidity present only as a hint.

entries.clue: Go back inside prison, maybe,  start of some expectation (9)

indicatorNotes.back: Something sent back travels the other way, so the two letters beside it are written in reverse.
indicatorNotes.inside: What is inside a thing sits within it, so the piece named goes into the middle of the letters around it.
indicatorNotes.maybe: A thing that is only maybe so is not settled, and letters left unsettled are free to be re-set in another order.
indicatorNotes.start of: The start of a word is its opening letter, and nothing beyond that letter is taken.

blocks.note: six letters to be re-set, and they part to take the reversed pair between them
the word taken whole and then read the other way about
the opening letter of the word, which is all that is asked for

annotation.surface: A man going back to jail, with some idea of what he can expect.
annotation.walkthrough: Inside is British for in prison, which keeps the whole sentence reading as a repeat offender's story. A prognosis is the forecast of how an illness will run, the sequel to the diagnosis.
annotation.definitionFit: A prognosis is a doctor's forecast of how a case will turn out, so expectation names what it is: what is expected rather than what is known.

entries.clue: So icy, when screwing, hard – and rather evasive (6)

indicatorNotes.screwing: Screwing a thing round twists it out of position, and letters twisted like that land in none of their old places.

blocks.note: five letters to be re-set
H is the grading stamped on a hard pencil

annotation.surface: A lover cold to the touch, hard going in bed and giving little away.
annotation.walkthrough: Screwing is the smut in the picture and the plainest possible instruction underneath it. Coyish is coy with the edge taken off: holding back from an answer rather than refusing one.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone coyish will not give a straight answer, which is evasiveness in a mild degree — the rather doing the softening.

entries.clue: It's unrefined and offensive to puncture contraceptive (5,3)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer instead of naming it, an adjective standing where a noun is wanted, with it doing duty for the answer itself.

indicatorNotes.to puncture: To puncture a thing is to pierce it and end up inside, so the letters named go within the word that follows.

blocks.note: the coil is the intrauterine device a doctor fits; the word parts after its first letter
rude talk is offensive talk

annotation.surface: Somebody coarse and offensive enough to put a hole in a contraceptive.
annotation.walkthrough: The coil is the loop a doctor fits inside the womb, and it is the word being punctured here. Unrefined is meant literally: straight out of the well, before any refinery has touched it.
annotation.definitionFit: Crude oil is petroleum as it comes out of the ground, so unrefined names the state that tells it from everything made of it.

entries.clue: Wrongful war – er, Donald Trump's not much bothered about it (3,3,5)

annotation.definition: Trump's not much bothered about it
annotation.definitionNote: The definition points at the answer through a jibe rather than naming it: the thing the man claims to stand for and, the setter says, ignores.

indicatorNotes.Wrongful: What is wrongful is not as it ought to be, so the letters beside it are set down in an order that is not theirs.

blocks.note: eleven letters to be re-set, the hesitation counting as two of them

annotation.surface: A botched war, and a president who cannot be bothered about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The er is a stammer on the page and two of the letters to be re-set, which is where the length comes from. The sting is all in the definition: what the man in the clue campaigned on twice and, in the setter's view, cares little for.
annotation.definitionFit: Trump ran for office promising law and order while facing prosecutions of his own, so the clue names the answer by the gap between the slogan and the conduct.

entries.clue: (& 25ac.) It's often broken by politicians' lacking self-awareness – or my entire works (5)

annotation.definition: It's often broken by politicians' lacking self-awareness
annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer by what keeps happening to it rather than naming it, the joke being that the thing is imaginary in the first place.

indicatorNotes.works: When a thing works its parts are all in motion, and letters in motion do not stay where they were put.

blocks.note: ten letters to be re-set, taken as they stand

annotation.surface: A complaint about what politicians keep breaking, with an author throwing in his collected writings.
annotation.walkthrough: The gauge in the definition is a joke instrument: people say theirs has exploded when somebody says something self-contradicting without noticing. My entire works reads as a writer's output and is only a heap of letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An irony meter is the imaginary instrument people claim to have broken when a speaker contradicts himself and hears nothing wrong.

entries.clue: Catchphrase of TV presenter with member flipped over (6)

indicatorNotes.flipped: A thing flipped is turned end for end, so the three letters beside it are written backwards.
indicatorNotes.over: What goes over something lies across it on both sides, so the letters just turned round close about the piece named.

blocks.note: a member is a limb, and the arm is the limb that fits; those letters are then read the other way about
Ant is Anthony McPartlin of Ant and Dec, the Geordie pair who have fronted Saturday-night television in Britain for thirty years

annotation.surface: A television presenter's pet saying, delivered with a limb flipped over.
annotation.walkthrough: Member is the limb here, not the thing Cyclops usually means by the word. Ant and Dec are always billed in that order, which is why the shorter half is the one crosswords use.
annotation.definitionFit: A mantra is a phrase somebody repeats until it stands for them, which is the work a catchphrase does for a performer.

entries.clue: Healthy state of my north-eastern paramilitary force (8)

blocks.note: my! and well! are the same small cry of surprise, so either stands for the other
the compass point in its two-letter form
the SS, the Schutzstaffel, was the Nazi party's own armed corps

annotation.surface: A man boasting about the fitness of his private army up north.
annotation.walkthrough: My is an exclamation rather than a possessive, which is the swap the whole clue turns on. The Schutzstaffel began as Hitler's bodyguard, and its two letters are crossword shorthand for any sinister force.
annotation.definitionFit: Wellness is the state of being well in body and mind, the word health clinics prefer, so healthy state says the same thing plainly.

entries.clue: (& 19ac.) Bitter period: Conservative, past it, needs break (4)

blocks.note: C is the party's letter on a ballot paper
somebody past it is too old for whatever it was
a dry stick breaks with a snap, and the noun does for the break itself

annotation.surface: An ageing Tory in a foul temper who could do with a holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: Bitter is the weather word, not the beer or the mood, and the period wanted is a stretch of days. Past it is the unkind English for too old to manage, which is where the surface gets its sourness.
annotation.definitionFit: A cold snap is a short spell of bitter weather, so the definition names its temperature and its shortness at once.

entries.clue: Last month with speaker who papers over the cracks? (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names the answer by what he does, with who standing in for one who, and the question mark covers an idiom being taken at face value.

blocks.note: December is the last month of the year, in the three-letter form a calendar prints
an orator is a public speaker, the one who addresses a crowd

annotation.surface: A December speech-maker smoothing over the year's failures.
annotation.walkthrough: Papering over the cracks is the idiom for hiding a fault instead of mending it, and the joke is the one tradesman who does it with actual paper. The question mark is the setter admitting as much.
annotation.definitionFit: A decorator hangs wallpaper for a living, so he papers over cracks in a wall in the literal sense the idiom borrowed.

entries.clue: Guts shown by boozers holding a doctor back (7)

indicatorNotes.holding: Something held is kept inside, so the drinkers' letters part and take what follows between them.
indicatorNotes.back: Taken back, the two letters named are written in the opposite order.

blocks.note: a boozer is a pub and an inn is the crossword's pub; more than one adds the S, and the word parts after the third letter
the article taken as it stands
Dr is the title in front of a doctor's name, and the two letters are then read the other way about

annotation.surface: Pub regulars showing courage by holding a doctor back from something.
annotation.walkthrough: Guts is bravery in the picture and the plain plural in the definition, the stuff inside. Boozer is British for the pub itself as well as for the man propping up its bar.
annotation.definitionFit: Innards is the homely word for the insides of a body or a machine, which is what guts means when it is not courage.

entries.clue: Leer at a tit (no time, sadly, to reciprocate) (9)

indicatorNotes.no time: Saying there is no time takes time out of what is in front of you, and t is the letter time comes down to.
indicatorNotes.sadly: Something done sadly is done badly, and letters handled badly do not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: ten letters with one t struck out by the instruction in the bracket, leaving nine to be re-set

annotation.surface: Someone ogled who is sorry to have no time to ogle back.
annotation.walkthrough: A tit is a small garden bird as well as the cruder thing, which is the cover the surface takes. The letter struck out is t for time, the one physics puts in its equations.
annotation.definitionFit: To retaliate is to do back what was done to you, which is reciprocating when what is being returned is an injury.

entries.clue: Mind Harry's protector (8)

blocks.note: to mind a shop is to watch it while the owner is out
to harry somebody is to dog them, chasing and worrying at them until they give way

annotation.surface: A warning to look out for the man guarding Harry.
annotation.walkthrough: Harry is the verb, not the prince: to harry is to keep after somebody without letting up. The second sense of the answer is the body appointed to keep an industry honest.
annotation.definitionFit: A watchdog guards the premises, and the word has spread to any body set up to guard the public interest, so protector covers it either way.

entries.clue: Smoke issuing from the woman grabbed by a numpty (7)

indicatorNotes.grabbed by: Somebody grabbed by another is caught inside their grip, so the letters before go within the word that follows.

blocks.note: a silly old coot is a fool, and numpty is British for the same harmless idiot; the word parts after its first letter
the woman named as the object of a sentence

annotation.surface: Smoke rising off a woman who has been grabbed by an idiot.
annotation.walkthrough: Numpty is British, Scots to begin with, for a harmless fool, and the coot of the wordplay is the bird in silly old coot. A cheroot is the cigar cut square at both ends, the kind smoked in Burma and Manila.
annotation.definitionFit: A cheroot is a cigar open at either end, and a smoke is what anybody calls the cigar they are about to light.

entries.clue: see 13ac.
Messenger, in leather, mesmerises (6)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in something sits inside it, so the letters wanted lie unbroken within the words that follow.

blocks.note: the letters run on from the end of one word into the start of the next, in the order they are written

annotation.surface: A courier in a leather jacket who holds everybody spellbound.
annotation.walkthrough: The hiding place runs straight across a comma, where the eye least wants to look. Hermes carried messages for the gods of Olympus in winged sandals, and the parcel firm took its name from him.
annotation.definitionFit: Hermes was the herald of the Greek gods, the one who fetched and carried for Zeus, so messenger is the post he held.

entries.clue: Johnny, getting end away, partied – shameless! (8)

indicatorNotes.getting end away: Getting the end away sends the last letter off, so the name beside it finishes one letter short.

blocks.note: Johnny Depp the film actor, docked of the last letter of his surname
to rave is to party the night out, which is where the rave got its name

annotation.surface: A man called Johnny having it off and then going out dancing.
annotation.walkthrough: Getting your end away is British for having sex, and a johnny is a condom, so the sentence is filthy twice over before the film star turns up. The exclamation mark is mock outrage and carries no instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody depraved is corrupt and past caring who sees it, which is shamelessness carried as far as it goes.

entries.clue: Somewhat oversexed composition (5)

indicatorNotes.Somewhat: Somewhat means in part, so part of what is written is wanted rather than the whole of it.

blocks.note: the letters sit unbroken inside the word, beginning at its second letter

annotation.surface: A rather randy piece of writing.
annotation.walkthrough: A single word carries the whole hiding place, which is harder to see than letters running across a gap. Composition means poetry here, not a piece of music or a school essay.
annotation.definitionFit: Verse is writing in metre, so composition names it as a made piece of work rather than by any synonym.

entries.clue: It's left of stage with a gutless celebrity (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition says what the answer is rather than naming it, the it standing for the answer and left being the past of leave.

indicatorNotes.gutless: Something gutless has had its middle taken out, so only the letters at either end are left standing.

blocks.note: a leg of a race or a journey is one stage of it
the article taken as it stands
the first and last letters of the word, with everything between them gone

annotation.surface: Somebody standing stage left beside a spineless celebrity.
annotation.walkthrough: Left of stage is a position on a theatre floor in the picture and the past of leave in the definition. Gutless works twice over: cowardly on the surface, hollowed out in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A legacy is what somebody leaves behind them, money in a will or a reputation after office.

entries.clue: Good 'rush' from this vice? (5)

blocks.note: G is the single letter for good, the mark on a school report
a rush is a tall marsh plant, and a reed is the same stuff standing in the same water

annotation.surface: The good rush somebody gets out of a bad habit.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks mark rush as a word wanted for its plant sense rather than the drug high the surface offers. This vice points at the answer itself, so the clue defines and builds the same word in one breath.
annotation.definitionFit: Greed is one of the seven deadly sins, so vice names the class it belongs to rather than offering a synonym.

entries.clue: see 10ac.
Goes into the back of goal – Foster's all round! (4-4)

indicatorNotes.all round: Something all round a thing encircles it, so the letters part and take the piece named between them.

blocks.note: to foster a child is to rear it, so fosters and rears are the same verb; the letters part after the fourth
a goal is the end somebody is working towards

annotation.surface: A goal going in at the back of the net, with Foster's for everybody.
annotation.walkthrough: Foster's is the Australian lager, and all round is a round of drinks for the bar, which is the picture the surface wants. The verb in the definition came over from America and is now the usual British word for the prang.
annotation.definitionFit: To rear-end a vehicle is to drive into the back of it, so the definition spells out the collision the verb names.

entries.clue: One who seizes role of loan shark (without power) (7)

indicatorNotes.without: Without carries its older sense of outside, as in without the city walls, so the letters named close round the letter that follows.

blocks.note: a loan shark lends at extortionate interest, which is the usurer's trade; the word parts after its fourth letter
P is the physicist's letter for power, the one on a light bulb's rating

annotation.surface: Somebody moving in on a moneylender's patch now that he has no clout left.
annotation.walkthrough: Without reads as lacking in the bracket and means outside in the wordplay, which is the whole difficulty of the clue. What gets seized in the definition is a throne or an office belonging to somebody else.
annotation.definitionFit: A usurper takes a throne or an office by force and holds it without right, so one who seizes names the act he is known by.

entries.clue: Sailor who's experienced a dose: "Awfully good!" (3,3)

indicatorNotes.Awfully: Something done awfully is done badly, and letters badly handled do not keep the order they came in.

blocks.note: five letters to be re-set
G is the single letter for good, the mark on a school report

annotation.surface: An old salt who has picked up a dose of something and is calling it marvellous.
annotation.walkthrough: A dose is a clap of venereal disease in sailors' English, which is what the quotation marks are enjoying. Awfully good is one phrase on the page and two separate jobs underneath it.
annotation.definitionFit: A sea dog is a sailor who has spent his life at sea, so the definition is about the years behind him rather than any rank.
